This document is part of the WHO guidelines titled Consolidated Strategic Information Guidelines for Viral Hepatitis Planning and Tracking Progress Towards Elimination. It is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes, as required by WHO's guideline development process. The document was developed by Dr. Yvan Hutin and Dr. Tomoyuki Hayashi from WHO's Global Hepatitis Programme, with contributions from a scientific committee. Members of the committee include Dr. Francesco Negro, Dr. Erika Duffell, Dr. Yusuke Shimakawa, Dr. Helena Cortez Pinto, and Dr. Antons Mozalevskis. Background on Mortality Data and Viral Hepatitis Surveillance WHO proposes a comprehensive approach to viral hepatitis surveillance, focusing on three key areas: (1) acute hepatitis, reflecting new infections; (2) the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections; and (3) mortality from sequelae such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Reducing mortality from HBV and HCV infections is one of the two criteria for defining the elimination of hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, as outlined in the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS). Therefore, countries need methods to measure mortality associated with HBV and HCV infections. In the early 2000s, WHO's mortality estimates for viral hepatitis only accounted for deaths from acute infections, as these were directly reported with their own International Classification of Disease (ICD-10) codes. This approach overlooked the majority of deaths secondary to cirrhosis and HCC, which were reported under separate ICD codes without reference to hepatitis. Since 2010, the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) project has developed estimates of worldwide mortality secondary to chronic HBV and HCV infections, accounting for deaths from chronic hepatitis sequelae based on their viral causes. This was achieved by estimating the proportion of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to HBV and HCV infections at national, regional, and global levels using published studies. WHO and GBD now use this approach to estimate mortality. Need for National Mortality Estimates At the national level, most countries lack systematic processes to generate mortality estimates for viral hepatitis. To address this, countries need to institutionalize methods previously used in ad-hoc studies and integrate them into routine surveillance systems. Generating national estimates of hepatitis-related mortality requires two steps: (1) estimating mortality from chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis and HCC) and (2) estimating the fraction of these conditions attributable to various hepatitis viruses. National mortality data are usually available, but in countries with suboptimal vital registration systems, estimates from WHO or GBD can be used. In countries where hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection is a public health concern, the prevalence of HBV/HDV coinfection in HBV-infected patients with cirrhosis and HCC should also be estimated. This information can be used to calculate the fractions of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to HBV, HCV, and HBV/HDV infections, which can then inform national hepatitis mortality rates. Objectives of Surveillance The objectives of the surveillance protocol include: Recruiting a representative sample of patients with cirrhosis and HCC. Assessing the HBV, HCV, and HDV status of these patients through medical record reviews. Estimating the proportion of patients with cirrhosis and HCC who have HBV, HCV, or HDV infections. Estimating the proportion of patients dying from or undergoing liver transplantation for cirrhosis and HCC who have HBV, HCV, or HDV infections. Providing data for national estimates of mortality due to viral hepatitis sequelae. Surveillance Activities The population under surveillance includes patients with cirrhosis or HCC hospitalized or seen as outpatients in referral hepatology or gastroenterology centers. Investigators at participating centers will identify clinicians to function as investigators for surveillance activities. ICD-10 codes may be used to identify patients in healthcare facilities. Cirrhosis cases are classified as probable (defined by ultrasound or non-invasive tests) or confirmed (defined by pathological evidence from liver biopsy). Late-stage liver disease due to chronic viral hepatitis is clinically defined by the presence of decompensated cirrhosis (e.g., jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, variceal bleeding) and/or HCC. HCC cases are defined according to the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) guidelines, using imaging criteria or pathological evidence. Data Collection and Analysis Data will be extracted from patient records using a case report form. Information collected will include age, sex, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome components (e.g., weight, diabetes), and HBV, HCV, and HDV infection status. Rare risk factors for cirrhosis and HCC will be aggregated as other causes. Investigators will not be directly involved in patient care within the departments where data are collected. The analysis plan includes estimating the attributable fraction of cirrhosis and HCC cases due to HBV, HCV, and HDV infections. Time trends in the fraction of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to these infections will be analyzed to assess the impact of new antiviral treatments. National mortality estimates will be derived by applying the attributable fraction to national mortality data for cirrhosis and HCC. Data Ownership Data generated through this surveillance protocol will be managed and owned by the sentinel centers that generate them. These centers will adhere to national obligations, rules, and regulations regarding data management and sharing.
